5b305bf5a2:
The guide words this objective as "trade-offs among built-in tools, custom tools, Skills and MCPs". In practice the questions draw on every extension point of Claude Code, the Agent SDK and the API: built-in tools, custom tools, MCP servers, Skills, slash commands, subagents, hooks, CLAUDE.md and rules files, and plugins that bundle them.

This chapter doesn't re-teach how to write any of them. Instead, it gives each mechanism a profile on six axes:

  • what problem it solves;
  • when it enters the context window, and what that costs;
  • who invokes it;
  • how deterministic it is;
  • who can share it;
  • what it costs to maintain.

Then it turns those profiles into a decision procedure and runs the procedure on fourteen worked cases. It builds one capability three different ways and prices each. It ends with the anti-patterns the exam uses as distractors.
4a060f3028: Reading time: about 2.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 18 runnable examples: ccdvf-companion/23-agentic-customization/ (run bash run_all.sh; all offline). It contains the decision engine with a test table and a context-cost calculator. Under samples/ you'll find a sample Skill, command, subagent, hook, rules, CLAUDE.md and plugin files, with a validator for each.
9a932edb67:
Neighbouring chapters, for the mechanics:

  • chapter 09 sections 13 to 15 cover plugins on each surface;
  • chapter 10 covers settings files and scopes;
  • chapter 11 covers CLAUDE.md, rules, Skills, commands and subagents in Claude Code;
  • chapter 20 covers hooks as a safety layer;
  • chapter 21 covers writing custom tools;
  • chapter 22 covers MCP servers.

Here we only choose between them.
d0f75feb6e:
Every extension point changes exactly one of six things about an agent: what it can reach (built-in tools, custom tools, MCP servers), what it knows (CLAUDE.md, rules, Skills), how a person starts a workflow (slash commands, user-invoked Skills), where work happens (subagents), what is guaranteed regardless of what the model decides (hooks and permission rules), or how all of that is distributed (plugins).

Choosing well means naming which of the six you need, then picking the mechanism in that row that loads into context as late as possible, is invoked by the right party, is as deterministic as the requirement demands, and is shared at the right scope, while costing the least to keep working.
7bb3c519a5:
At 4.1% of 53 items, this objective is worth two or three direct questions. The reasoning shows up in many more, though. A large share of Claude Code and agent questions are really "which mechanism" questions in disguise.

The official sample that belongs here is the inventory REST API used by many applications. The answer is an MCP server.

The distractors follow stable patterns:

  • a prompt or CLAUDE.md line offered where a guarantee is needed;
  • an MCP server offered for something that is only knowledge;
  • a custom tool that duplicates a built-in;
  • an always-loaded file offered for something needed once a month;
  • a subagent offered for a two-line lookup.

Once you can say which row a requirement lives in, most of those options eliminate themselves.
3fdad03e72: None of these mechanisms is new as an idea. Each one is an old extension pattern from editors, shells and build systems, re-applied to a program whose "user" is a language model with a finite context window. Know the ancestor and you know what each one is for. The ancestors' failure modes are mostly the same failure modes, too.
215d546b04:
Run-control files. Unix shells read .profile and .bashrc at startup. Editors read .vimrc or init.el. Git reads .gitconfig at user and repository level. The pattern is a text file at a known path, loaded every time, layered from global to local.

CLAUDE.md (introduced with Claude Code in February 2025) is the same idea for a model. It's a file read at session start, layered from organisation to user to project to directory. Its failure mode is the old one as well. An rc file that grows to two thousand lines slows every start, and nobody knows which lines still matter.
64109176eb:
Hooks. Git hooks (pre-commit, pre-push), Emacs hook variables and web framework middleware all let you attach code to a lifecycle event that the host fires. The hook runs whether or not the user remembers it.

Claude Code hooks (mid-2025) attach shell commands, HTTP calls, prompts or agents to events such as PreToolUse and Stop. The defining property carries over from Git: the host runs the hook, not the actor being constrained.
bc4aa6932f:
Commands and macros. Editor macros, shell aliases, Makefile targets and IDE "live templates" let a person trigger a stored sequence by name. Claude Code slash commands (.claude/commands/*.md) are stored prompts, started by typing /name.

In 2026 the docs describe custom commands as merged into Skills. A file in .claude/commands/deploy.md and a folder .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy.
304ad46b12:
Plugins and packages. VS Code extensions, Eclipse plugins, Maven artifacts and npm packages bundle several extension points with a manifest and a version. You install them from a registry.

Claude Code plugins (late 2025) bundle Skills, agents, hooks and MCP server definitions under .claude-plugin/plugin.json. They're installed from a marketplace listed in .claude-plugin/marketplace.json.
6b3799e979:
Language-model specific steps. Tool use (2024) gave the model typed actions. The Model Context Protocol (November 2024) made a tool server a reusable process that many clients can connect to. Subagents gave a model the equivalent of a worker process with its own memory.

Agent Skills (October 2025) added the one idea with no exact ancestor: progressive disclosure. Only a one-line description is always present. The body, reference files and scripts are pulled in by the model when a task matches.

The closest older analogy is lazy class loading in the JVM. The class name is known; the bytecode is loaded on first use.
04e183d5c2:
Before comparing mechanisms, classify the requirement. A requirement asks for one of six things, and the six don't substitute for each other.

This is the single most useful step on the exam. The four options in a "which mechanism" question are usually drawn from different rows, and only one row matches the requirement.
60765cb3f4:
Some requirements span two rows and need two mechanisms. Take "Claude should review PRs our way, and the reviewer must never push". That's Knowledge plus Guarantee: a Skill for the checklist, and a deny rule or hook for the push. The exam likes these, and the wrong options typically solve one half.

A good habit is to underline the verbs in the scenario:

  • "knows", "follows", "uses our format" point to Knowledge;
  • "must", "never", "always", "guarantee", "compliance" point to Guarantee;
  • "several applications", "other teams", "reuse" point to a shared capability or to Distribution.
049c8caa07: The row decides most of the answer. The six axes in the next section decide between mechanisms inside a row: a custom tool versus an MCP server, say, or CLAUDE.md versus a Skill.
e8be3cc65d:
Within a row, compare mechanisms on six axes. Do the same across rows when a requirement is ambiguous. The objective text asks for trade-offs, and these are the trade-offs.

Each axis has a physical cause in how the harness and the model work. Know the cause, and you can answer questions about mechanisms you haven't memorised.
16dcc702d2: State it as the row from section 03, plus the narrower job inside the row. A built-in tool and an MCP server both give capability. But the built-in tool solves "generic local operations Claude already knows how to use". The MCP server solves "a system outside the process that several clients need".
f2f2a09a74:
The context window is shared, finite and paid per request (chapter 16). Every request in an agent loop re-sends the system prompt, all tool definitions and the conversation so far. So anything that is always present is paid on every turn, multiplied by the number of turns, multiplied by the number of sessions.

Prompt caching (chapter 15) cuts the price of a stable prefix to about a tenth for cache reads. It doesn't reduce the space taken, though. And space is the scarcer resource, because attention over long contexts degrades (see chapter 16's lost-in-the-middle material).

The mechanisms fall into five loading classes:
6aef272022: Always, in full: CLAUDE.md files above the working directory, their @imports, and .claude/rules/ files without a paths field. The docs recommend under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. They also note that imports organise a file but don't reduce its cost, because imported files load at launch too.
3572f189c9: Always, as definitions: tool definitions (built-in, custom, MCP) are sent with every request. A definition with a good description is typically 100 to 400 tokens. Claude Code enables MCP tool search by default. That defers MCP tool definitions and loads them when a search finds them; check the docs for the current thresholds and the ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH values. On the API, defer_loading plus the tool search tool does the same for your own tools (chapter 21).
9aef48da50: Always, as a one-line listing: each Skill contributes its name and description. So does each subagent and command Claude can invoke on its own. The API Skills overview puts this at about 100 tokens per Skill. In the listing, Claude Code truncates a Skill's combined description and when_to_use at 1,536 characters.
4ffc96ff0c: On demand: a Skill body loads when invoked (the API docs say under 5k tokens; the Claude Code docs recommend SKILL.md under 500 lines). Reference files load when read. Scripts run, and only their output enters context. Path-scoped rules and subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load when Claude works with matching files. A command body loads when the user types it.
2dc9d6fc7c: Elsewhere or nowhere: a subagent's work happens in its own context window, and only its final message returns to the parent. A hook runs in the harness and costs zero model context. The exception is a hook that deliberately returns text for Claude (for example additionalContext or a block reason), and that text is small and targeted.
07ba40509b:
One subtlety the exam can test: a subagent saves the parent's context, not money. The subagent's own tokens are billed.

Say a subagent reads 150k tokens of logs and returns 800 tokens. That costs 150k input tokens either way. What it buys is a parent conversation that stays at 800 rather than 150k for every later turn. The parent's attention isn't diluted either.
24b53850c2:
There are three possible invokers:

  • The model decides to call a tool, read a Skill or delegate to a subagent, based on descriptions.
  • The user types a slash command, mentions a subagent with @, or runs claude --agent.
  • The harness fires hooks on events and loads CLAUDE.md at startup, with no decision by anyone in the moment.

Configuration can push several mechanisms between invokers. A Skill with disable-model-invocation: true can only be started by the user. One with user-invocable: false is hidden from the / menu, so only Claude can start it.

Model invocation is convenient but probabilistic; it depends on the description matching the request. User invocation is deliberate but depends on someone remembering. Harness invocation depends on neither.
9cd0c58bec:
How certain is it that the behaviour happens, once it's configured?

Hooks and permission rules are deterministic. The harness evaluates them on every matching event, and the model can't talk its way past them. Exit code 2 on PreToolUse blocks the call, and a JSON "permissionDecision": "allow" printed in the same hook can't override that.

Tool execution is deterministic code, but tool selection is the model's choice.

Everything in the Knowledge row is advisory. The memory docs say it directly: Claude treats CLAUDE.md "as context, not enforced configuration". To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, you use a PreToolUse hook.

Prompts have a non-zero failure rate even when well written. For most conventions that's fine. For safety and compliance it isn't.
967c155ddc:
Each mechanism has scopes. Most have four:

  • a personal scope (~/.claude/...);
  • a project scope committed to the repository (.claude/..., .mcp.json, root CLAUDE.md);
  • a local-only project scope (.claude/settings.local.json, CLAUDE.local.md, MCP "local" scope in ~/.claude.json);
  • an organisation scope through managed settings.

Plugins add a distribution scope that crosses repositories: one versioned bundle installed into many projects from a marketplace.

MCP servers running remotely add a scope that crosses clients. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, claude.ai connectors and your own SDK agents can all use the same server.

Skills on the API are workspace-wide once uploaded. On claude.ai they're per user. Custom Skills don't sync between surfaces.
88eb5de254:
This axis is what it costs to keep the mechanism correct after day one.

Markdown (CLAUDE.md, rules, Skills, commands, subagent definitions) is cheap to change but rots silently. Nothing fails when a convention changes and the file doesn't.

Code (custom tools, hooks, MCP servers, Skill scripts) can be tested. It must be tested, versioned and kept compatible with the harness, too.

A remote MCP server is a service. It needs deployment, authentication, monitoring and an owner.

Plugins add release management and a trust review for every consumer, since a plugin runs with the user's privileges.
128abe50a5:
Problem solved. Generic local capability:

  • reading, searching and editing files (Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep);
  • running commands (Bash);
  • fetching and searching the web (WebFetch, WebSearch);
  • delegating (the Agent tool, formerly called Task);
  • tracking work (todo/task tools).

On the API, Anthropic also defines client tools you execute (bash, text editor, computer use, memory) and server tools it executes (web search, web fetch, code execution, tool search). Chapter 21 section 16 covers them.
64319c925f: Loading and cost. Their definitions are always present in Claude Code and the Agent SDK. You don't choose their wording, so there's no description work. You do choose which ones are enabled: allowedTools/disallowedTools in the SDK, permission rules in settings, and tools lists on subagents.
8a53724099: Invoker and determinism. The model chooses them. Their implementation is deterministic and tested by Anthropic. Claude has also been trained on these exact interfaces, and that's the strongest argument for them. A custom read_file with your own schema is a tool the model has never seen, and it will use it less fluently than Read.
16fe247da4: Scope and maintenance. They're available everywhere Claude Code or the SDK runs, with zero maintenance for you. What you maintain is the permission policy around them: which Bash commands are allowed, and which paths can be written.
7de096d8d6:
Choose it when the capability is generic and local. If you find yourself writing a custom tool that reads files, runs shell commands or fetches URLs, stop. Restrict the built-in one instead.

The exam phrasing is often "the team built a custom tool to search the repository". The better answer uses Grep and Glob with a permission rule.
529bce676f:
Problem solved. A capability specific to one application: your billing service's credit endpoint, a calculation in your codebase, a lookup in a database only this agent uses.

On the raw Messages API, you define the tool and run it in your dispatcher (chapter 21). In the Agent SDK, you write an in-process tool, typically with the @tool decorator and create_sdk_mcp_server. That exposes it to the agent through an in-process MCP server, without a separate process.
456e1b6330: Loading and cost. The definition is in every request of that application, typically 100 to 400 tokens each. Ten custom tools come to a few thousand tokens per turn before caching.
b0aa93d902: Invoker and determinism. The model selects it from its description. Your code executes it deterministically, and your dispatcher can enforce validation, approval and limits (chapter 21 sections 13 and 17).
91c6029c2d:
Scope and maintenance. The tool lives inside one application, and that's its main limitation. The second application that needs the same capability must copy the code, the description and the error model. Then the copies drift.

Maintenance is ordinary code maintenance plus description maintenance. The description is a routing input, so changes to it need an eval (chapter 21 section 08).
166d8fdfe2:
Choose it when exactly one application needs the capability, it's tightly coupled to that application's state (an in-memory session, a transaction), and it isn't generic.

Move it to MCP when a second consumer appears, when the system belongs to another team, or when a service should hold the credentials rather than each app.
e59a8b1098:
Problem solved. A capability that many clients need, packaged once behind a standard protocol. As chapter 22 explains, that means tools (model-controlled actions), resources (application-controlled data) and prompts (user-controlled templates).

The official CCDV-F sample answer is this row exactly: "an inventory REST API reused across several apps should be exposed as an MCP server".

Vendors ship servers for standard systems (GitHub, Jira, Slack, databases). So for a standard system, the first question is whether a maintained server already exists.
f22ad4c267:
Loading and cost. Each server's tool definitions are added to every request of every client connected to it, unless tool search defers them. In Claude Code, MCP tool search is the default. It keeps a large server's definitions out of context until a search surfaces them. In your own SDK or API agent, you get the same effect with deferred loading and the tool search tool.

Results cost context too. Claude Code warns when an MCP tool result exceeds 10,000 tokens and limits it to 25,000 by default (MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS). An MCP server whose tools return 20k-token JSON blobs is a context problem, however its definitions load.
a63e52b38c:
Invoker and determinism. Tools are model-invoked. Prompts are user-invoked (they appear as slash commands in Claude Code). Resources are attached by the application or the user. Execution is deterministic server code.

A server can enforce authorisation, rate limits and audit centrally. That's a real advantage over N copies of a custom tool, each with its own checks.
e4ee299f50:
Scope and maintenance. In Claude Code, you configure a server at one of three scopes, as chapter 22 and chapter 10 show:

  • local scope (default, private, ~/.claude.json);
  • project scope (.mcp.json committed, shared with the team);
  • user scope (all your projects, private).

A remote Streamable HTTP server is reachable from any MCP client.

Maintenance is the highest of any mechanism. You have a process or service to deploy, secure (OAuth for remote servers, chapter 20 section 20), version and monitor. And the tool descriptions must stay good enough that the agent doesn't prefer a built-in instead.
bf6b7354d3:
Choose it when the capability is an external system, several clients or teams need it, credentials and audit should be central, or a maintained server already exists.

Do not choose it to deliver knowledge. An MCP server with a get_style_guide tool that returns static Markdown is a Skill with a process attached. It costs a definition on every turn, a server to run, and a tool call to read text. A Skill would have loaded that text only when relevant.
e5690cf000:
Problem solved. Packaged know-how: a procedure, a house format, a checklist, domain rules, with optional reference files, templates and scripts. A Skill is a folder with SKILL.md (YAML frontmatter, then instructions) and anything else it needs.

Anthropic's own material puts it in one line: MCP gives Claude access, Skills give Claude expertise.
af0d44332b:
Loading and cost: progressive disclosure. There are three levels.

Level 1 is the name and description. It's always present, at about 100 tokens per Skill.

Level 2 is the body of SKILL.md. It loads when Claude decides the Skill applies or the user invokes it. Keep it under 5k tokens (API docs) or under 500 lines (Claude Code docs).

Level 3 is bundled files, and they cost nothing until accessed. Reference files enter context when read. Scripts are executed, and only their output enters context.

That last point is the reason to put deterministic work in a script inside the Skill rather than describing it in prose. Think filling a PDF form, validating a CSV, computing a checksum. The script is reliable, and its source never costs a token.

In Claude Code, a loaded Skill body stays in the conversation. After compaction, the most recent invocation of each Skill is re-attached, up to 5,000 tokens each within a 25,000-token combined budget.
b05149867b:
Invoker. Both, by default. Claude loads a Skill when the request matches its description, and the user can type /skill-name. Frontmatter shifts this:

  • disable-model-invocation: true makes it user-only (deploy, release, anything with side effects you want started deliberately);
  • user-invocable: false makes it model-only background knowledge;
  • paths limits automatic activation to matching files;
  • context: fork runs the Skill in a subagent, with agent selecting the subagent type.
0f24fa8e58:
Determinism. Selection is probabilistic and depends on the description, the same way tool selection does (chapter 21 section 08). Instructions inside are advisory. Scripts inside are deterministic once run.

A Skill can also register hooks in its frontmatter, active for the rest of the session once invoked. It can list allowed-tools that pre-approve tools for the invoking turn. Neither makes the Skill itself mandatory.
f118df9bcc:
Scope and sharing. Each surface handles this differently.

  • Claude Code: personal ~/.claude/skills/, project .claude/skills/, nested directories, enterprise managed settings, and plugins (namespaced /plugin-name:skill-name). On name collisions, enterprise beats personal and personal beats project.
  • API: uploaded through the Skills API (/v1/skills) and workspace-wide. Skills run inside the code execution tool's container, and the request names the Skill in the container parameter. Anthropic's pre-built Skills are pptx, xlsx, docx and pdf.
  • claude.ai: per user.

Custom Skills don't sync between these surfaces. The Agent SDK can load filesystem Skills; check the docs for the exact option names that enable them.

The API has name rules. A name is at most 64 characters of lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens, with no XML tags, and it can't contain "anthropic" or "claude". The description must be non-empty and at most 1,024 characters. It should say both what the Skill does and when to use it.
88ba8a2a2e:
Maintenance. Markdown plus optional scripts. It's cheap to edit, and the scripts should have tests. The description is a routing input and deserves the same care as a tool description.

Treat third-party Skills like installing software: audit every file. Be wary of Skills that fetch from external URLs, since fetched content can carry instructions (chapter 19).
85f76332ba: Choose it when the requirement is knowledge or procedure that some sessions need but not all, that runs longer than a few lines, or that comes with files or scripts. It's the default answer for "the team wants Claude to follow our X procedure".
499d64b719:
Problem solved. A person wants to start a known workflow deliberately and by name: /review, /release-notes v4.2, /fix-issue 1234.

The body is a stored prompt with argument substitution ($ARGUMENTS, $0, named arguments). It can also use dynamic context injection. A line such as !`git diff HEAD` runs a command before the prompt reaches Claude and splices in its output.
610befbf2f:
Relationship to Skills. In current Claude Code, custom commands have been merged into Skills. .claude/commands/review.md keeps working and behaves like a Skill named review. A Skill folder adds supporting files, frontmatter controls and automatic loading. If both exist with the same name, the Skill wins.

For new work, the practical difference comes down to one decision. Should Claude also be able to start this on its own? If not, it's a Skill (or command file) with disable-model-invocation: true.

MCP servers can also publish prompts, which Claude Code exposes as slash commands. That's the route when the command belongs to a shared server rather than to a repository.
06618fe631: Loading and cost. A user-only command costs nothing until typed. With model invocation disabled, it isn't in the model's listing at all. Once typed, its body loads once.
dffe6e5424: Invoker and determinism. The user. Invocation is deterministic in one sense: typing /review always loads the same prompt. What Claude then does with it is as probabilistic as any prompt. Dynamic context injection is deterministic, because the command runs before the model sees anything.
224b674bfd: Scope and maintenance. Personal or project, like Skills; namespaced in plugins. Shared commands in .claude/commands/ or .claude/skills/ are checked into VCS. That's the official CCAR-F sample answer for "make a command available to the whole team". Maintenance is low.
c87dde9752:
Choose it when the workflow has a clear start that a human controls. That goes double if it has side effects (deploy, publish, open a PR) or is expensive.

Don't rely on a command when the behaviour must happen without someone remembering to type it. If it must happen, that's a hook. If it should happen when relevant, that's a model-invocable Skill.
2576e09528:
Problem solved. Doing work in a separate context window, with its own system prompt, tool set, model and permissions, and returning only a result. Two different problems lead here.

The first is context. A verbose task (exploring an unfamiliar codebase, reading test logs, scanning 300 files for a pattern) would flood the main conversation. So it runs elsewhere and returns a summary.

The second is role: a reviewer that may only read (tools: Read, Grep, Glob), a test runner on a cheaper model, a security auditor with its own instructions.
6b0aaef7c6:
Mechanics in brief (chapter 11 section 09 has the details). Subagents are Markdown files with frontmatter. They live in .claude/agents/ (project), ~/.claude/agents/ (personal), a plugin's agents/ directory, or managed settings, or come from the --agents flag. Only name and description are required.

Useful fields:

  • tools (allowlist; inherits everything if omitted) and disallowedTools;
  • model (sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, a full ID, or inherit);
  • permissionMode;
  • skills (preloaded in full);
  • hooks, maxTurns, mcpServers, isolation: worktree.

The built-ins are Explore (read-only, fast codebase search), Plan (read-only research in plan mode) and general-purpose.

A subagent starts with a fresh context: its system prompt, the task message the parent writes, CLAUDE.md files, a git status snapshot and its preloaded Skills. It doesn't see the parent's conversation, so everything it needs must be in the task message. Only its final message returns. By default, nesting is allowed up to three layers below the main conversation.
3a3f06a7cc:
Loading and cost. Its name and description sit in the parent's listing. Its work costs its own tokens, billed in full, in a window the parent never sees. The parent pays only for the task message it writes and the summary it receives.

Start-up has a cost too. Every subagent re-reads CLAUDE.md and has to rediscover context the parent already had. So a subagent for a two-step lookup costs more, and is slower, than doing it inline.
ad0dcabc03:
Invoker and determinism. The model delegates based on the description. Phrases such as "use proactively after code changes" in the description make delegation more likely. Or the user asks explicitly: by name, by @-mention, or by starting a whole session with claude --agent name.

The tool restriction is deterministic: a subagent without Edit cannot edit. Whether the subagent gets used is not.
867023ca99: Scope and maintenance. Personal, project, plugin or managed. Plugin subagents ignore hooks and permissionMode in their frontmatter. Remember that when a plugin's reviewer appears to ignore its hooks. Maintenance is low (Markdown), but a subagent's system prompt and tool list need the same review as any agent.
1babd5fdfb:
Choose it when the work is verbose relative to its result, needs a different tool set or model, or should run in parallel with other work.

Do not choose it in three cases. The task is small. The task needs the conversation's full history (that's a fork, not a fresh subagent). Or the requirement is a guarantee: a "safety subagent" that the main agent may or may not consult enforces nothing.
c783aede6c:
Problem solved. Something must always or never happen, regardless of what the model decides. Examples: block rm -rf or writes to prod.env, run the formatter after every edit, refuse to stop while tests fail, log every tool call for audit, inject today's on-call rota at session start.

Chapter 20 teaches writing them safely. The point here is when to choose one.
12fe77f3c3:
Mechanics in brief. You configure hooks in several places: settings files (user, project, local, managed), a plugin's hooks/hooks.json, Skill frontmatter (active for the rest of the session once invoked), or subagent frontmatter (active while that subagent runs).

There are five handler types:

  • command (shell, JSON on stdin);
  • http;
  • mcp_tool;
  • prompt (a single-turn model evaluation);
  • agent (a subagent that can use tools; experimental).

There are many events. PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SessionStart and SubagentStop come up most.

For PreToolUse, exit code 2 blocks the call, and stderr becomes the reason Claude sees. JSON output can return a permissionDecision of allow, deny, ask or defer.

Default timeouts are 600 seconds for command, http and mcp_tool handlers, 30 for prompt, and 60 for agent. The Agent SDK has the same model as Python or TypeScript callbacks (HookMatcher).
baa042805f: Loading and cost. The hook itself takes zero model context. It does cost wall-clock time on every matching event. That matters for hooks on PostToolUse of every Edit.
e32fdc6869:
Invoker and determinism. The harness. A command hook is as deterministic as its script. A prompt or agent hook puts a model call inside the hook: the hook always runs, but its verdict is a model judgement.

Use those for checks that need judgement ("does this commit message describe the change?"). Never use them as the only control for something that must not happen.
dfd1f35567:
Scope and maintenance. Personal, project (committed), local, managed (organisation-wide, can't be overridden by users), plugin.

Maintenance is real code. Test it with recorded inputs and keep it fast. Decide what happens when it crashes (chapter 20 section 10). Parse commands instead of pattern-matching strings (chapter 20 section 07).

For a fixed pattern, a deny rule in permissions is often simpler than a hook. Hooks are for logic a pattern can't express.
728fd02376:
Choose it when the requirement contains "must", "never", "always", "every time", "compliance", or describes an action whose failure is expensive.

Do not choose it to teach a procedure. Picture a hook that rejects every non-conforming test file with a 40-line stderr message. That's a Skill written in the most expensive way possible: the model learns the convention by failing at it.
7f897cd7c2:
Problem solved. Facts and conventions Claude needs in most sessions: build and test commands, repository layout, naming conventions, "we use Gradle, not Maven", "integration tests need Docker running".

Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/*.md with a paths glob handle conventions that apply to one kind of file wherever it lives. Examples are **/*.test.ts or src/main/java/**/*Controller.java. Chapter 11 sections 03 to 05 cover the hierarchy, imports and rules mechanics.
b055b313a0:
Loading and cost. CLAUDE.md files above the working directory and unconditional rules load at launch, in full, every session. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files and path-scoped rules load on demand, when Claude works with matching files. Root CLAUDE.md is re-read and re-injected after /compact.

Target under 200 lines per file; Claude Code skips a file over 4 MiB. @imports (up to four hops deep) organise content but don't save tokens, because they load at launch too. Auto memory (MEMORY.md, which Claude writes) loads its first 200 lines or 25KB.
3a7c49ce38: Invoker and determinism. The harness loads it, and the model treats it as advisory context. Specific, concise instructions are followed more consistently than long, vague ones. Contradictory instructions in different files produce arbitrary results.
59943d6de5: Maintenance. Cheap to edit, expensive to neglect. Every line is paid in every session. So ask of each line: "is this needed in most sessions?" If not, it belongs somewhere else. That's a path-scoped rule if it's needed when touching certain files, a Skill if it's needed for certain tasks, or nowhere at all.
bc9bfecfab:
Problem solved. Distribution. A plugin is a directory with a manifest at .claude-plugin/plugin.json and any of skills/, agents/, hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json and other components. It's installed and enabled as one unit, usually from a marketplace (a repository containing .claude-plugin/marketplace.json).

A plugin is not a new kind of capability. Everything in it works on its own without a plugin. What it adds is versioning, one-step install, updates and namespacing (/my-plugin:review), so bundles from different teams don't collide. Chapter 09 sections 13 to 15 cover plugins across surfaces.
134469f025:
Loading and cost. The sum of its parts, in every session where it's enabled. Not only the sessions where you use it.

Each model-invocable Skill, agent and command adds its listing line every turn. Its MCP servers run as processes and add tool definitions, subject to tool search. Its hooks fire on their events.

The /plugin interface shows a context-cost estimate for plugins in Anthropic's official marketplace. It also shows a "Not used recently" group for plugins you could disable.
1a54d999b6: Invoker and determinism. Inherited from each component. Installing a plugin is a deliberate user or admin action. Managed settings can force-install plugins, and allowlist or block marketplaces.
f7be5f3bcd:
Scope. User (every project on this machine), project (enabled for everyone through committed .claude/settings.json, though each collaborator still installs it), or local (you, this repository).

The same plugin format also installs on claude.ai and in Cowork, where a different set of components loads; check the platform support table in the docs. Cloud sessions don't load plugins from your local settings.
bef6d4e0ea: Maintenance. Release management (versions, changelog, compatibility), a marketplace to host, and trust. A plugin runs with the installing user's privileges, so consumers should review it like any dependency. Plugin subagents ignore their own hooks and permissionMode fields.
e79a0395d2: Choose it when you're shipping several components together to people in more than one repository, or want versioned releases. Do not choose it for one Skill used in one repository. Commit .claude/skills/x/ and you're done.
279695612f: Here are the profiles above, side by side. Learn the columns as reasons rather than as cells. The exam rarely asks for a cell. It asks which mechanism a scenario's constraints point to.
2b095ed594:
The loading classes become concrete when you put numbers on them. The figures below are estimates for reasoning: about 4 characters, or about 0.75 words, per token for English prose, with tool definitions measured from typical well-described tools. The companion calculator, 04_context_cost_calculator.py, lets you change every input.

The documented anchors are about 100 tokens per Skill listing, Skill bodies under 5k tokens, CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, and MCP results warned at 10k and capped at 25k by default.
c290d9a5c2: A team pastes its release-note procedure, with three worked examples, into the root CLAUDE.md. It's about 600 lines, roughly 7,500 tokens. Sessions in this repository average 40 model requests. (An agentic session re-sends context on every request, not on every human message.) Release notes get written in about one session in twenty.
f9999350a8:
In CLAUDE.md, every session pays 7,500 tokens on each of 40 requests. That's 300,000 input tokens per session, spent on text relevant to one session in twenty.

Prompt caching bills the stable prefix at roughly a tenth after the first write. So the money cost drops to the equivalent of roughly 30,000 to 40,000 tokens per session (cache reads plus the first cache write). The space doesn't drop, though. Every request in every session carries 7,500 tokens of release procedure, competing for attention with the code being edited.

Adherence to the other CLAUDE.md lines also tends to fall as the file grows. That's why the docs give the 200-line target.
34e0f72441:
As a Skill, every session pays about 100 tokens on each of 40 requests for the listing: 4,000 tokens.

In the one session in twenty that writes release notes, the body loads when needed, say at request 20. It's then present for the remaining 20 requests: 150,000 tokens in that session.

Averaged over twenty sessions, that's 4,000 + 150,000 / 20 = 11,500 tokens per session. That's about 26 times less than the uncached CLAUDE.md figure. And the examples can go into examples.md inside the Skill, read only if the model needs them, which cuts the loaded body further.
e7b5e4b634:
The crossover is worth knowing. Suppose the procedure were needed in nearly every session, from the first request. Then the Skill would cost about the same as CLAUDE.md (the listing plus the body for the whole session). It would also add the risk that the model fails to load it.

So knowledge needed early in almost every session belongs in CLAUDE.md, as long as it's short. The later in a session the body typically loads, the further the break-even moves in the Skill's favour. The calculator prints the break-even usage rate for any size and load point.
740dff5d32:
A developer connects a project-management MCP server with 30 tools, about 250 tokens each with descriptions and schemas: 7,500 tokens. Without deferred loading, that's the same 7,500 tokens per request as case A, in every session, for a server used in a few sessions a week.

With MCP tool search (the Claude Code default), the definitions aren't loaded up front. A search tool finds the relevant ones when the model needs them, and only those definitions enter context.

The lesson for the exam: "connect fewer servers" and "defer tool loading" are both correct mitigations. "Move the 30 tools into CLAUDE.md as documentation" is not, because the model then knows about tools it can't call.
0ac7a05986:
Say you need every caller of a deprecated BillingClient.charge() overload across a 2,000-file monorepo. That might take 60 Grep and Read calls and about 120,000 tokens of results.

Inline, those results stay in the main conversation. The next 30 requests each carry them (until compaction), and the agent does its later work with 120k tokens of search noise in its window.

In an Explore-style subagent, the subagent pays the 120k. The parent receives a 1,500-token list of call sites, grouped by module. Total tokens billed are slightly higher with the subagent (task message, its own CLAUDE.md load, the summary). But the parent's next 30 requests each carry 1.5k instead of 120k.
4eb8553163:
A line "never run rm -rf" in CLAUDE.md costs about 10 tokens per request and works most of the time. A PreToolUse hook costs zero tokens and works every time it's reached.

Here the comparison isn't about tokens at all. The cheaper mechanism is also the one that gives the guarantee. That's why cost is axis 2 and not axis 1: the row decides first.
cac7ba0912: The procedure below orders the questions so the most expensive mistakes get caught first. A guarantee satisfied by advice fails silently in production. A capability built at the wrong scope gets copied and drifts. Knowledge put in the always-loaded file costs every session, forever. Isolation and packaging are layered on top of whichever mechanism the first three questions chose.
03b47cd5b5: Must it always or never happen, whatever the model decides? Then it needs a harness mechanism. Use a permission deny rule if a fixed pattern expresses it (Bash(rm -rf:*)-style rules; check the docs for the exact rule syntax). Use a command hook if it needs logic: parse arguments, check a path, look up a ticket. Use a prompt or agent hook only if it needs judgement and a judgement is acceptable. Put it in managed settings if the organisation must enforce it and users must not override it. You may also add a short CLAUDE.md line explaining the rule, so the model doesn't waste attempts. But that line is documentation, not the control.
6a25d6d137: Does the agent need to reach a system or perform an action it cannot today? If a built-in tool can do it, use the built-in and restrict it with permissions. If not, ask four things. Does more than one client, application or team need it? Does the system belong to someone else? Should credentials and audit be central? Does a maintained MCP server already exist? Any yes points to an MCP server: remote if several machines or clients, project .mcp.json if one repository's developers. All no points to a custom tool in that one application.
0f290dba3a: Does the agent need to know something or follow a procedure? If it's short, stable and needed in most sessions, use CLAUDE.md (personal preferences go in user CLAUDE.md). If it applies to certain files wherever they live, use a path-scoped rule. Otherwise use a Skill, with scripts for any step that must be exact and reference files for material needed only sometimes.
8e132de94c: Should a person start it deliberately? Make it user-invocable (a command file or a Skill). Add disable-model-invocation: true if it has side effects or cost that the model's own judgement should never trigger. If Claude should also pick it up when relevant, leave model invocation on and write the description for routing.
b1ca4aa2c3: Who else needs this, and how? Same repository: commit the files (.claude/, .mcp.json, CLAUDE.md). Several repositories or versioned releases: a plugin from a marketplace. The whole organisation, with enforcement: managed settings, possibly force-installing the plugin. One person: the user-level paths.
0ebba6e9fc:
Two tie-breakers settle most remaining choices.

Load as late as possible: among mechanisms that satisfy the requirement, prefer the one that enters context later. That means path rule over CLAUDE.md, Skill over CLAUDE.md, and deferred tools over always-loaded ones.

Prefer what already exists: built-in over custom, a maintained MCP server over writing one, an Anthropic pre-built Skill over re-implementing document generation.
295b981bac: The companion's 02_decision_engine.py encodes this procedure as a function. It takes a requirement record and returns a list of mechanisms with reasons. The record holds booleans such as must_always_happen, needs_external_system, consumers, sessions_needing_it, applies_to_paths, human_starts_it, side_effects and verbose. 03_decision_cases.py runs the fourteen cases below as a test table. The core of it is short:
5a65bd04e6: The thresholds (half the sessions, 30 lines) are teaching values, not documented constants. The documented guidance is the 200-line file target and "needed in most sessions". What matters is the order of the questions, and that a requirement can produce several choices.
e5311cf83d: Requirement. A platform team has a 120-line review checklist: error handling with Resilience4j, no blocking calls in reactive handlers, idempotency keys on POST, log redaction. They want every developer's Claude Code to review PRs against it, started with /review. Reviews must not modify code.
d16d7b6949: Choice. A project Skill, .claude/skills/review/SKILL.md, holding the checklist. It's user-invocable, with context: fork and agent: code-reviewer. Alongside it, a project subagent .claude/agents/code-reviewer.md with tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash(git diff *)-style read-only access (check the docs for tool-pattern syntax in the tools field). Both are committed to the repository.
e7651c4c2b:
This is the Knowledge row (the checklist), plus Invocation (/review), plus Isolation (a read-only role that keeps the diff analysis out of the main thread).

  • Loading: about 100 tokens idle, with the checklist loaded only when reviewing.
  • Invoker: the user, though Claude can also offer it when asked to review.
  • Determinism: the subagent's tool list enforces the read-only constraint. That's the only part that has to be certain.
  • Scope: project, shared through VCS.
  • Maintenance: one Markdown file the team edits in PRs.
b370b181b6: Rejected. CLAUDE.md: 120 lines in every session for a task done a few times a week. An MCP server returning the checklist: a service to run for static text. A hook: it can't apply a checklist that needs judgement, and the requirement doesn't say "must block".
30a67fe4e7: Requirement. Three consumers need the inventory service's REST API: a customer-care agent built on the Agent SDK, developers in Claude Code, and an analytics team using Claude Desktop. Calls must be authorised per user and audited.
f46b2260b3: Choice. A remote MCP server (Streamable HTTP, OAuth). It exposes a small set of well-described tools such as inventory_get_stock and inventory_reserve, plus resources for the catalogue. Developers add it to the repository's .mcp.json, with environment-variable expansion for the URL.
c9eccefb72: This is the Capability row, with three consumers on three clients. It's the strongest case for MCP, and the official sample answer. Authorisation and audit sit in one service instead of three copies. Loading: definitions per request, deferred by tool search in Claude Code; keep results small. Maintenance: high, but paid once instead of three times.
68f4bd91f5: Rejected. A custom tool in each application: three copies, with drifting descriptions and authorisation. A Skill with curl commands: credentials in every client, no central audit, and a Skill is knowledge, not access. Documenting the API in CLAUDE.md: the model learns about an API it still can't call safely.
a3556c98a1: Choice. A PreToolUse command hook on Bash that parses the command and exits 2 with a reason. It uses shlex and handles sudo, xargs, find -delete and bash -c. Add permission deny rules for the simple patterns. Put both in managed settings, so users can't remove them.
72e981ad2a: Guarantee row. Only the harness can make it impossible. The injected README is exactly the case where a prompt rule fails (chapter 19). Managed scope, because "any developer machine" and "impossible" rule out user-editable settings. Zero tokens. Maintenance: a tested script (chapter 20 sections 06 and 07).
bf3fee7bb8: Rejected. A CLAUDE.md line: advisory, and defeated by injection. A "safety" subagent: the main agent may never call it. A Skill describing safe deletion: knowledge, not control. Relying on plan mode: a mode a user can leave.
c92e06fd4f: Requirement. Finance onboards suppliers by filling a W-9-style PDF and a bank-details form from a supplier record. The field mapping has 40 rules: which name goes where for sole traders versus companies, date formats, checkbox values. Claude Code users in finance and an API-based onboarding agent both need it.
c2ce44711a:
Choice. A Skill with three parts: SKILL.md with the decision rules for ambiguous fields, field_map.md as a reference file, and scripts/fill_form.py, which writes the fields and validates the result.

In Claude Code, use project or plugin scope. On the API, upload the same Skill through the Skills API and run it with the code execution tool. (The pre-built pdf Skill can do the low-level PDF work.)
d286b8159c:
Knowledge row, with exact steps. The script makes the filling deterministic and costs no context. Only the rules the model must judge are prose. Progressive disclosure keeps the 40-rule map out of context until a form is filled.

Note the surfaces. A Claude Code Skill and an API Skill are uploaded separately and don't sync.
71619f7a35: Rejected. An MCP server with a fill_pdf tool: possible, but then the mapping rules must live in the tool description or the server, and you run a service for a document procedure. It's reasonable only if many non-Claude systems also need it. CLAUDE.md: 40 rules in every session. A custom tool in the API agent only: Claude Code users get nothing.
53ba7289d6: Requirement. Before a Spring Boot 2 to 3 migration, an architect asks Claude Code to find three things across 1,800 files: every use of javax.* packages, every WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter subclass, and every custom HandlerInterceptor. Then it should plan the migration in the same session.
a506794df3: Choice. Delegate the search to the built-in Explore subagent, or to a custom read-only subagent with a structured return format (file, line, construct, module). Keep the planning in the main conversation, ideally in plan mode.
1a427f41c9: Isolation row: the search is verbose relative to its result. The parent keeps a compact inventory instead of 100k tokens of grep output, so it plans with a clean window. The subagent's tools are read-only, so nothing changes during discovery.
bdd101caf0: Rejected. Doing it inline: the planning then runs in a window full of search results. A custom find_usages tool: Grep and Glob already do it. A Skill: the requirement isn't knowledge.
24f7248ae1: Requirement. Test files must use AssertJ, given/when/then naming and Testcontainers for database tests. That covers *Test.java under src/test in 30 modules, plus **/*.test.ts in the web app. The conventions are 25 lines.
d55014e04c: Knowledge row, keyed by file type across directories. That's what paths exists for (the CCAR-F 3.3 official answer). The rules load only when Claude works with matching files, so a session that never touches tests pays nothing. They're shared through VCS.
1a7b1decd4:
Rejected.

  • CLAUDE.md: paid in sessions that never touch tests.
  • A CLAUDE.md in each of 30 test directories: duplicated, and it drifts.
  • A Skill: it works, but the conventions should apply whenever a test file is touched, not when a description happens to match the request.
  • A hook that rejects non-AssertJ tests: that enforces style by failure, and the requirement says "use", not "must be impossible to violate".
acf7b294e3: This is knowledge needed in nearly every session, short and stable. It's the one thing CLAUDE.md is for. The loading cost is small and paid where it's useful.
3377d25d7d: Rejected. A Skill: the model would have to load it in almost every session, and might not. A slash command: someone has to remember it.
2cbb47cc46: Choice. A PostToolUse hook matching Edit|Write that runs ./gradlew spotlessApply on the changed file (or a faster formatter call). It's committed in project settings.
57ac4b5f1f: "After every edit", "always": that's the harness row. The formatter is deterministic, so the guarantee is cheap. It takes zero tokens. Latency per edit is the cost, so keep it to the changed file.
c12765b2bb: Rejected. A CLAUDE.md line "run spotless after editing": sometimes skipped, and it costs a model turn each time it isn't. A Skill. A command the developer types at the end: forgotten.
322baa436c: Requirement. Release managers want /release 4.2.0 to bump versions, generate the changelog from merged PRs, tag, and open the release PR. It must never start just because Claude thought it was a good idea.
f17a9fbb5d: Choice. A project Skill, .claude/skills/release/, with disable-model-invocation: true and argument-hint: [version]. It uses allowed-tools to pre-approve the git and gh commands it needs for that turn, and it includes a changelog script. Optionally, add a PreToolUse hook that denies git push --tags unless the branch is main.
3eda9d7181: Invocation row, with side effects. User-only invocation is the whole point. The Skill gives the script and the procedure a home. The hook adds the one guarantee that matters.
ae0548cc4c: Rejected. A model-invocable Skill: it could trigger on "let's get this released soon". CLAUDE.md instructions: no trigger, and always loaded. An MCP prompt: only if the workflow belonged to a shared server.
4fcd4f53bb: Requirement. A billing chatbot built on the Messages API keeps a draft plan change in the user's session object. Before confirming, it needs the model to compute proration against that draft.
433937fd34: This capability is needed by one application and coupled to its in-memory state. An MCP server would need the session state passed across a process boundary, for no consumer's benefit. The definition costs a few hundred tokens per request.
8ceb099c8d: Rejected. An MCP server: no second consumer, and the state lives in the app. A Skill with a script: the API agent would need code execution, and the script wouldn't see the session object.
af5d8c4214: Requirement. The developer-experience team wants every service repository to get four things, with versioned updates: the review Skill and reviewer subagent from case 1, a secrets-scanning PreToolUse hook, and the Jira MCP server. Security requires the secrets hook everywhere.
ff9c40bf14:
Choice. A plugin (skills/review/, agents/code-reviewer.md, hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json) in an internal marketplace. Enable it at project scope in each repository's .claude/settings.json, or force-install it through managed settings.

The security-required hook also goes in managed settings. Plugin subagents ignore hook fields, and a user can disable a plugin.
b4c0c1827d: Distribution row, across repositories, with versions: exactly what plugins are for. The guarantee part sits at the scope that can enforce it.
7fdc3a8fa1: Rejected. Copying files into 40 repositories: drift. A plugin alone for the security hook: a plugin can be disabled, and enforcement belongs in managed settings.
e86bf14e14: Choice. The Anthropic pre-built xlsx Skill through the API. That requires the code execution tool and naming the Skill in the container parameter. Add a custom Skill, uploaded through the Skills API, for the house report layout.
552882f852: This is knowledge plus a script-based capability in a sandbox, already built and maintained by Anthropic. Prefer what exists.
6823578b09: Rejected. A custom tool that builds spreadsheets with openpyxl: now you own a document generator. An MCP server for spreadsheet writing: a service for a single agent's output format.
d21e15cf68: Requirement. A team wrote a custom MCP tool, search_repo(query), that shells out to ripgrep. They find Claude uses it inconsistently.
52f9670d3f: A built-in that Claude is trained on already covers this capability. The custom tool adds a definition to every request and competes with Grep for the same requests. That's the overlap problem from chapter 21 section 18.
bace15050f: Rejected. Improving the custom tool's description. That fixes the routing symptom but keeps the duplication.
6a9e43a4ca: Choice. The maintained GitHub MCP server, configured in project .mcp.json with the token taken from an environment variable (never committed). Or the gh CLI through Bash with a permission rule. Use whichever the team already uses.
16abde76d7: This is a standard external system, so prefer an existing server over writing one (CCAR-F 2.4). Project scope shares the configuration without sharing credentials.
b0bc8b4e13: Rejected. Writing an in-house GitHub MCP server. Putting a token in CLAUDE.md or .mcp.json (chapter 20).
903dd54505:
The requirement: "Claude should be able to look up an order's status in the order management system (OMS) by order id." Three engineers build it three ways, and all three work in a demo.

They differ on every axis, though. Seeing the differences on one concrete capability is the best preparation for questions that describe one of them and ask what it costs.
11df686b10: The in-process server is an SDK convenience. The agent sees the tool through the MCP interface, but it runs inside the application process, and no other client can reach it. Check the docs for the exact is_error key and return shape in the SDK version you use.
510708e55a:
The script reads a token from the developer's environment and calls the same REST endpoint.

Note the extra value Way C carries that A and B don't: the interpretation rules for HELD_FRAUD and dates. That's knowledge. In A and B, it would have to be written into tool descriptions or the system prompt.
b7f4a79195:
Read the table as the exam does.

  • If the scenario says "the care agent, the developers and the analytics team", it's B.
  • If it says "only this agent, and it reads the in-memory basket", it's A.
  • If it says "developers occasionally need to check orders while debugging and must follow the rules about fraud holds", it's C. Probably C on top of B later: the Skill can call the MCP tool instead of a script, keeping the knowledge in the Skill and the access in the server.

That layered answer, MCP for access and a Skill for how to use it, is the most common correct design in practice.
74899cabde: The companion's 15_three_ways.py builds all three against a fake OMS and the fake client. It counts the tokens each adds to a 40-request session, with and without a lookup, and prints its own measured version of the table above. (Its chars/4 estimates come out somewhat lower than the round figures here.)
b02afdc5b8: Real features combine mechanisms, each doing the part it's good at. The pattern is stable enough to memorise: MCP for access, Skills for know-how, subagents for isolation, hooks for guarantees, CLAUDE.md for the few facts every session needs, and a plugin to ship the bundle. Most bad designs come from mixing up which layer does which job.
4d2591c58d:
Take the review feature from case 1, extended for a whole department. A developer types /acme-review:review 2481.

The Skill body loads. A dynamic-context line in it runs gh pr diff 2481, so the diff arrives without a model turn. The Skill has context: fork and agent: code-reviewer, so the review runs in the read-only subagent. That subagent also has the Jira MCP server's jira_get_issue tool, to check that the PR matches its ticket. It returns a structured list of findings.

Meanwhile, a PreToolUse hook from managed settings blocks any gh pr merge during the session.

The plugin ships the Skill, the agent and the Jira server definition. The merge-blocking hook sits in managed settings, because it must hold even if someone disables the plugin.
993113e3e3:
You could push each part into another layer. Every such push makes the design worse:

  • the checklist in CLAUDE.md costs every session;
  • the Jira access as a Skill with curl spreads credentials;
  • the merge block as a line in the Skill is advice;
  • the review inline in the main thread fills it with the diff.
c6bae4e19c:
What's wrong here? Two tool definitions ride in every request of every connected client. There's a process to deploy and keep alive. And a tool call drops a full 9,000-token document into context when only one section was needed.

The model also has to decide to call a tool to read guidance. It does that less reliably than it loads a matching Skill. The fix moves the knowledge to where knowledge goes:
e1494b8d5b: So when is a server returning documents right? When the documents are dynamic or permissioned, like a knowledge base searched per user with access control. Or when non-Claude clients need them too. That's a search capability, not a style guide.
f92f02d8c7:
The fix follows the procedure line by line. Guarantees go to hooks, file-type conventions to path rules, occasional procedures to Skills, and the rest gets deleted.

The companion's 12_claude_md_linter.py flags the patterns automatically:

  • files over 200 lines;
  • sections with imperative "NEVER/ALWAYS/MUST" (candidate hooks);
  • sections mentioning file globs (candidate rules);
  • long sections with procedural numbered steps (candidate Skills).
49ea2cea98: Keep a one-line note in CLAUDE.md ("pushes to main are blocked by a hook; open a PR"). That way the model plans around the rule instead of discovering it by being blocked. Chapter 20 covers the harder parsing cases (bash -c, xargs, chained commands) and what to do when the hook crashes.
93c22b935b: The custom versions each cost a definition. They overlap with the built-ins the model prefers, so routing becomes inconsistent. They lose the built-ins' permission integration and safety work. And they give the model unfamiliar interfaces. Custom tools are for capabilities that don't exist yet.
b121228b17:
Selection runs on the description, exactly as tool selection does. A description should say what the Skill does, and when to use it, in the words users actually type. It should also say what files or situations trigger it.

The API limits it to 1,024 characters. Claude Code truncates description plus when_to_use at 1,536 in the listing. So put the key use case first.
2ccd427d55:
The subagent starts cold. It re-reads CLAUDE.md and has to rediscover which service and which file the parent already knew. Then it returns a summary the parent has to trust. Inline, this is one Grep and one Read.

When delegation is right (case 5), the task message must carry the goal, the constraints, what's already been found, and the return format. The subagent doesn't see the conversation.
e3972f09c9:
A deploy Skill without disable-model-invocation: true can load just because a conversation mentioned deploying. Anything with production side effects, cost or irreversibility should be user-invoked. Where it must also be safe, guard it with a hook or permission rule.

The broken and fixed versions differ by one frontmatter line. That's why the exam can test it in one sentence.
170c24a60b:
Picture a PostToolUse hook that rejects every test file not using AssertJ, with a 40-line stderr explaining the conventions. It teaches the model by failure. Each violation costs a wasted edit, a block message in context and a retry.

Put the convention in a path rule, so the first attempt is right. Keep a hook only if violations must be impossible, and for style they rarely must be.
43d34d05e9: Packaging one Skill used in one repository as a plugin adds a manifest, a marketplace, versioning and an install step for each developer. All that, to replace a committed folder. Plugins pay off across repositories or for external distribution.
8e4e94625a:
Think of a Skill script with a hard-coded token, an .mcp.json with a literal API key, or a CLAUDE.md that says "use token abc123". Customization files are shared by design, so they're the worst place for secrets.

Use environment-variable expansion in .mcp.json, OAuth for remote MCP servers, and per-user credentials read at run time (chapter 20 sections 16 to 20).
325e739bb8:
Here's a frequent trap: an option names a mechanism that doesn't exist on the surface the scenario uses.

CLAUDE.md, slash commands, hooks configured in settings files and plugins are Claude Code features. (The Agent SDK can load the filesystem configuration when told to.) An application built on the raw Messages API has none of them. Its "CLAUDE.md" is the system prompt. Its "hooks" are code in your dispatcher. Its "subagents" are separate API calls you orchestrate.

The table maps each need to its form on each surface. Chapter 09 section 04 has the longer version.
940b6be909: The principle carries across surfaces even when the names change. On the raw API, "use a hook" means "enforce it in your dispatcher before executing the tool". "Use a Skill" means either the API Skills feature or, more simply, loading a procedure into the prompt only for requests that need it. The exam rewards recognising the principle under a different name.
466b88b3da: Every mechanism has a characteristic failure. Most of them map back to the axis the designer ignored. When a scenario says "the team added X but Claude still does Y", find the axis.
935f48f91e: If you've spent years in Spring, most of these mechanisms have a familiar counterpart. The counterpart usually predicts the trade-off correctly.
c2e495c6e7: The analogy that misleads is CLAUDE.md as configuration. The framework enforces application.yml. CLAUDE.md is read by a model that may or may not follow it. Treat CLAUDE.md like a README the model reads every time. Treat hooks and permission rules as the actual configuration.
a78f64f0ed: Exam scenarios phrase the maintenance-cost axis as "six months later". The mechanisms age differently.
bf9e0c8f9f:
Markdown rots without failing. A Skill that says "use the v2 billing endpoint" keeps loading after v2 is retired. Nothing breaks until the model follows it.

Practical controls:

  • an owner per Skill and rule file (CODEOWNERS on .claude/);
  • review in the same PR as the code change that invalidates it;
  • a periodic check that every path and command named in the Markdown still exists (the companion's validators do the path check).
e22279c3d6:
Code customizations need tests. Hooks, Skill scripts and MCP servers are code that the harness runs. Test hooks with recorded event JSON (chapter 20 section 13). Test scripts like any CLI. Test MCP servers with the inspector and contract tests (chapter 22).

A hook that crashes on unexpected input either blocks everything or, worse, silently allows everything. Which one depends on how it fails.
cd628c3fda: Routing needs evals. Skill and tool descriptions are routing inputs, and changing one can steal traffic from a neighbour. Keep a small labelled set of requests per Skill ("should trigger", "should not trigger"), and run it when descriptions change. The plugins documentation describes testing plugins with evals.
9ee57531ea: Footprint needs measurement. Plugins, MCP servers and Skills accumulate, so review what's enabled. The /plugin interface lists plugins not used recently and shows context-cost estimates for official-marketplace plugins. /context-style views show what occupies the window (check the docs for the current command). MCP tool search keeps idle servers cheap, but not free.
9e450ea0f9:
Scope drift. Sometimes the whole team relies on one person's customizations: "it works on my machine because I have a user-level Skill". That's a scope bug.

The fix is promotion. User scope moves to project files. Project files move to a plugin when several repositories need them. Plugin hooks move to managed settings when they become policy.
41504d127d: Several consumers on different clients, plus central authorisation and audit: that's the definition of the MCP case, and it mirrors the official sample. A duplicates code and authorisation. B and D provide knowledge, not access, and B spreads credentials.
06707540b6: The requirement is a guarantee, so it needs the harness. A deny rule expresses a fixed path pattern. A hook is needed if "merged" requires logic, such as checking git history. A and C remain advisory, and D doesn't prevent anything.
c2a8257258: Path-scoped rules load only when Claude works with matching files, wherever they are, and they're maintained in one place. A costs every session. B duplicates and drifts. D teaches by failure, and enforces style that doesn't need enforcement.
74daf841a8:
With a Skill, knowledge used occasionally loads on demand. The exact step belongs in a script, whose source costs no context.

B pays every session. C runs a service for a document procedure and crams rules into a description. D only loads when typed and loses automatic use. It also has no place for the script beyond what a Skill offers.
e9e25f7f90: The work is verbose relative to its result, which puts it in the isolation row. The subagent pays for the search in its own window, and the parent keeps a compact inventory. A doesn't affect input context. C and D change neither where the tokens land nor the volume of results.
0285fa81a3: Plugins distribute versioned bundles across repositories. Managed settings enforce policy that users can't disable. C puts a must-hold control in something a user can disable. A drifts. D is unshareable and unenforceable.
3643f709ba: The capability already exists as built-ins that the model knows and that integrate with permissions. Duplicates cause overlap and lose the safety controls. A and C treat the routing symptom. D adds a service to the duplication.
